chunks: "The biggest difference is how they're controlled.
A BJT is current-controlled: a small base current into a forward-biased junction controls a larger collector current, with a gain beta around 100.
A MOSFET is voltage-controlled: the gate voltage sets up a channel across an insulating oxide, so the gate draws essentially no DC current, just a pulse of charge when you switch it.
That leads to the practical differences.
The BJT has a much higher transconductance for the same current, I C over V T , about 39 mS at 1 milliamps, because of its exponential law.
It also matches well and has low noise, so it's better for precision analogue, references and low-noise amps.
But it needs continuous base current, has a saturation voltage of around 0.
2 volts, and it has positive thermal feedback, because V BE drops as it heats, so parallel BJTs can run away.

The MOSFET has no gate current, a very high input impedance, and in the on-state it's a resistor, R DS(on) , as low as a few milliohms, so for switching currents of amps its conduction loss is much lower.
R DS(on) rises with temperature, so MOSFETs share current in parallel. And it's the basis of CMOS, so it scales to billions of transistors.
So: MOSFET for switching and digital, BJT for precision and high-gain analogue, and an IGBT if you need both for high voltage."
